### Early diplomatic career and marriage

[![Image 10: Man in dark suit](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/John_Quincy_Adams%2C_by_John_Singleton_Copley.jpg/250px-John_Quincy_Adams%2C_by_John_Singleton_Copley.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Quincy_Adams,_by_John_Singleton_Copley.jpg)

John Quincy Adams by [John Singleton Copley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Singleton_Copley "John Singleton Copley"), c.1796

[![Image 11: Woman in brown clothing](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Louisa_Catherine_Johnson_Adams_by_Gilbert_Stuart%2C_1821-26.jpg/250px-Louisa_Catherine_Johnson_Adams_by_Gilbert_Stuart%2C_1821-26.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Louisa_Catherine_Johnson_Adams_by_Gilbert_Stuart,_1821-26.jpg)

[Louisa Catherine Johnson Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisa_Catherine_Johnson_Adams "Louisa Catherine Johnson Adams") by [Gilbert Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Stuart "Gilbert Stuart"), c.1821-26

Adams initially avoided becoming involved in politics, instead focusing on building his legal career. In 1791, he wrote a series of pseudonymously published essays arguing that Britain provided a better governmental model than France. Two years later, he published another series of essays attacking [Edmond-Charles Genêt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond-Charles_Gen%C3%AAt "Edmond-Charles Genêt"), a French diplomat who sought to undermine President [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington")'s policy of neutrality in the [French Revolutionary Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolutionary_Wars "French Revolutionary Wars").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-20) In 1794, Washington appointed Adams as the [U.S. minister resident to the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_Netherlands "List of ambassadors of the United States to the Netherlands"). Adams considered declining the role, but ultimately took the position on the advice of his father.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-21) While abroad, Adams continued to urge neutrality, arguing that the United States would benefit economically by staying out of the ongoing French Revolutionary Wars.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-22) His chief duty in Amsterdam was to secure and maintain Dutch loans essential to U.S. finances. On his way to the Netherlands, he met with [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay"), who was then negotiating the [Jay Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Treaty "Jay Treaty") with Great Britain. Adams supported the Jay Treaty, but it proved unpopular with many in the United States, contributing to a growing partisan split between the [Federalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalist_Party "Federalist Party") of [Alexander Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton") and the [Democratic-Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party") of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-23) In 1794 he supported [John Skey Eustace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Skey_Eustace "John Skey Eustace") who wanted to return to the United States via the Netherlands.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-24)

Adams spent the winter of 1795–1796 in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), where he met [Louisa Catherine Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisa_Adams "Louisa Adams"), the second daughter of American merchant Joshua Johnson. In April 1796, Louisa accepted Adams's proposal of marriage. Adams's parents disapproved of his decision to marry a woman who had grown up in England, but he informed his parents that he would not reconsider his decision.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-25) Adams initially wanted to delay his wedding to Louisa until he returned to the United States, but they married in [All Hallows-by-the-Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Hallows-by-the-Tower "All Hallows-by-the-Tower") on July 26, 1797.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-26)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-28) Shortly after the wedding, Joshua Johnson fled England to escape his creditors, and Adams did not receive the dowry that Johnson had promised him, much to the embarrassment of Louisa. Adams noted in his own diary that he had no regrets about his decision to marry Louisa.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-29)

In 1796, Washington appointed Adams as the [U.S. minister to Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_Portugal "List of ambassadors of the United States to Portugal").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-30) Soon, however, John Adams defeated Jefferson in the [1796 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1796_United_States_presidential_election "1796 United States presidential election"). When he became president, the elder Adams appointed John Quincy as the [minister to Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_Germany "List of ambassadors of the United States to Germany") instead.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-31) Though concerned that his appointment would be criticized as [nepotistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism"), Adams accepted the position and traveled to the Prussian capital of Berlin with his wife and his younger brother, [Thomas Boylston Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Boylston_Adams_(1772%E2%80%931832) "Thomas Boylston Adams (1772–1832)"). The State Department tasked Adams with developing commercial relations with Prussia and Sweden, but President Adams also asked his son to write to him frequently about affairs in Europe.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-32) His advice that he regularly gave to his father based on his experiences on the ground in Europe proved particularly valuable during the [Quasi-War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-War "Quasi-War") with France, although President Adams also relied heavily on his official staff for such advice and not primarily on his son.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-33) In 1799, Adams negotiated a [new trade agreement between the United States and Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Amity_and_Commerce_(Prussia%E2%80%93United_States) "Treaty of Amity and Commerce (Prussia–United States)"), though he could never complete an agreement with Sweden.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-34) He frequently wrote to family members in the United States, and in 1801 his letters about the Prussian region of [Silesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silesia "Silesia") were published in a book titled _Letters on Silesia_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-35) During his time in Prussia, Adams befriended the German diplomat and writer [Friedrich von Gentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Gentz "Friedrich von Gentz"), whose work, _The Origins and Principles of the American Revolution, Compared with the Origins and Principles of the French Revolution,_ Adams would translate into English in 1800. In the [1800 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1800_United_States_presidential_election "1800 United States presidential election"), Jefferson defeated John Adams, and both Adams and his son left office in early 1801.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-36)

### U.S. senator from Massachusetts

On his return to the United States, Adams re-established a legal practice in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), and in April 1802 he was elected to the [Massachusetts Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Senate "Massachusetts Senate").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-37) In November of that year, he ran unsuccessfully for the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-38) In February 1803, the Massachusetts legislature elected Adams to the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). Though somewhat reluctant to affiliate with any political party, Adams joined the Federalist minority in Congress.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-39) Like his Federalist colleagues, he opposed [the impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment_of_Samuel_Chase "Impeachment of Samuel Chase") of Associate Justice [Samuel Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Chase "Samuel Chase"), an outspoken supporter of the Federalist Party.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-40)

Adams had strongly opposed Jefferson's 1800 presidential candidacy, but he gradually became alienated from the Federalist Party. His disaffection was driven by the party's declining popularity, disagreements over foreign policy, and Adams's hostility to [Timothy Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Pickering "Timothy Pickering"), a Federalist Party leader whom Adams viewed as overly favorable to Britain. Unlike other New England Federalists, Adams supported the Jefferson administration's [Louisiana Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase "Louisiana Purchase") and expansionist policies.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-41) Adams was the lone Federalist in Congress to vote for the [Non-importation Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-importation_Act "Non-importation Act") of 1806, which attempted to coerce Britain into ceasing its interference with American shipping as part of the ongoing [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars"). Adams became increasingly frustrated with the unwillingness of other Federalists to criticize British actions, including [impressment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressment "Impressment"), and he moved closer to the Jefferson administration. After Adams supported the [Embargo Act of 1807](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embargo_Act_of_1807 "Embargo Act of 1807"), the Federalist-controlled Massachusetts legislature elected Adams's successor several months before the end of his term, and Adams resigned from the Senate shortly thereafter.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-42)

While a member of the Senate, Adams served as a professor of logic at [Brown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University")[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-43) and as the [Boylston Professor of Rhetoric and Oratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boylston_Professorship_of_Rhetoric_and_Oratory "Boylston Professorship of Rhetoric and Oratory") at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"). Adams's devotion to classical rhetoric shaped his response to public issues, and he would remain inspired by those rhetorical ideals long after the neo-classicalism and deferential politics of the founding generation were eclipsed by the commercial ethos and mass democracy of the [Jacksonian Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonian_democracy "Jacksonian democracy"). Many of Adams's idiosyncratic positions were rooted in his abiding devotion to the [Ciceronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero "Cicero") ideal of the citizen-orator "speaking well" to promote the welfare of the polis.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-44) He was also influenced by the classical republican ideal of civic eloquence espoused by Scottish philosopher [David Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume "David Hume").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-45) Adams adapted these classical republican ideals of public oratory to the American debate, viewing its multilevel political structure as ripe for "the renaissance of Demosthenic eloquence". His _Lectures on Rhetoric and Oratory_ (1810) looks at the fate of ancient oratory, the necessity of liberty for it to flourish, and its importance as a unifying element for a new nation of diverse cultures and beliefs. Just as civic eloquence failed to gain popularity in Britain, in the United States interest faded in the second decade of the 19th century, as the "public spheres of heated oratory" disappeared in favor of the private sphere.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-46)

### Minister to Russia

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/1815_US_passport_-_LONDON.jpg/250px-1815_US_passport_-_LONDON.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1815_US_passport_-_LONDON.jpg)

1815 US passport issued by John Quincy Adams at London

After resigning from the Senate, Adams was ostracized by Massachusetts Federalist leaders, but he declined Democratic-Republican entreaties to seek office.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-47) In 1809, he argued before the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") in _[Fletcher v. Peck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher\_v.\_Peck "Fletcher v. Peck")_, and the Supreme Court ultimately agreed with Adams's argument that the Constitution's [Contract Clause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_Clause "Contract Clause") prevented the state of Georgia from invalidating a land sale to out-of-state companies.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-48) Later that year, President [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison") appointed Adams as the first [United States Minister to Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Ambassador_to_Russia "United States Ambassador to Russia") in 1809. Though Adams had only recently broken with the Federalist Party, his support of Jefferson's foreign policy had earned him goodwill with the Madison Administration.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-49) Adams was well-qualified for the role after his experiences in Europe generally and Russia specifically.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-50)

After a difficult passage through the [Baltic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea "Baltic Sea"), Adams arrived in the Russian capital of St. Petersburg in October 1809. He quickly established a productive working relationship with Russian official [Nikolay Rumyantsev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolay_Rumyantsev "Nikolay Rumyantsev") and eventually befriended Tsar [Alexander I of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_I_of_Russia "Alexander I of Russia"). Adams continued to favor American neutrality between France and Britain during the Napoleonic Wars.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-51) Louisa was initially distraught at the prospect of living in Russia, but she became a popular figure at the Russian court.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-52) From his diplomatic post, Adams observed the French Emperor [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon")'s [invasion of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Russia "French invasion of Russia"), which ended in defeat for the French.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-53) In February 1811, President Madison nominated Adams as an [Associate Justice of the United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_Justice_of_the_United_States_Supreme_Court "Associate Justice of the United States Supreme Court").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-54)[The nomination was unanimously confirmed by the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams_Supreme_Court_nomination "John Quincy Adams Supreme Court nomination"), but Adams declined the seat, preferring a career in politics and diplomacy, so [Joseph Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Story "Joseph Story") took the seat instead.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-55)

### Treaty of Ghent and minister to Britain

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Am%C3%A9d%C3%A9e_Forestier_-_Signing_of_Treaty_of_Ghent_%281814%29.jpg/250px-Am%C3%A9d%C3%A9e_Forestier_-_Signing_of_Treaty_of_Ghent_%281814%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Am%C3%A9d%C3%A9e_Forestier_-_Signing_of_Treaty_of_Ghent_(1814).jpg)

Adams (center) during the signing of the Treaty of Ghent

Adams had long feared that the United States would enter a war it could not win against Britain, and by early 1812, he saw such a war as inevitable due to the continued British interference with American shipping, which included impressing alleged [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") deserters from US merchantmen. In mid-1812, the United States declared war against Britain, beginning the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812"). Tsar Alexander attempted to mediate the conflict between Britain and the United States, and President Madison appointed Adams, Secretary of the Treasury [Albert Gallatin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Gallatin "Albert Gallatin"), and Federalist Senator [James A. Bayard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Bayard_(politician,_born_1767) "James A. Bayard (politician, born 1767)") to a delegation charged with negotiating an end to the war. Gallatin and Bayard arrived in St. Petersburg in July 1813, but the British declined Tsar Alexander's offer of mediation. Hoping to start negotiations at another venue, Adams left Russia in April 1814.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-56) Negotiations finally began in mid-1814 in [Ghent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghent "Ghent"), where Adams, Gallatin, and Bayard were joined by two additional American delegates, [Jonathan Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Russell_(diplomat) "Jonathan Russell (diplomat)") and former [Speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives")[Henry Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clay "Henry Clay").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-57) Adams, the nominal head of the delegation, got along well with Gallatin, Bayard, and Russell, but he occasionally clashed with Clay.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-58)

During the initial stages of negotiation, the British delegation pushed for the creation of an [Indian barrier state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_barrier_state "Indian barrier state") near the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes"). As this was designed to prevent the westward expansion of US colonizers, the American delegation unanimously rejected this offer, and their negotiating position was bolstered by the US victory at the [Battle of Plattsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Plattsburgh "Battle of Plattsburgh").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-59) By November 1814, the [Liverpool ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_ministry "Liverpool ministry") decided to seek an end to hostilities with the U.S. on the basis of _[status quo ante bellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Status\_quo\_ante\_bellum "Status quo ante bellum")_. Even though this meant the issue of impressment would not be resolved, Adams and his fellow commissioners had hoped for similar terms. The treaty was signed on December 24, 1814. The United States did not gain any concessions from the treaty but could boast that it had survived a war against the strongest power in the world. Following the signing of the treaty, Adams traveled to Paris, where he witnessed first-hand the [Hundred Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Days "Hundred Days") of Napoleon's restoration.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-60)

In May 1815, Adams learned that President Madison had appointed him as the [U.S. minister to the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom "List of ambassadors of the United States to the United Kingdom").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-61) With the aid of Clay and Gallatin, Adams negotiated a limited trade agreement with Britain. Following the conclusion of the trade agreement, much of Adams's time in London was spent helping stranded American sailors and prisoners of war.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-Kaplan_2014_pages=307%E2%80%9311,_318%E2%80%9320-62) In pursuit of national unity, newly elected president [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe") decided a Northerner would be optimal for the position of [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), and he chose the respected and experienced Adams for the role.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-63) Having spent several years in Europe, Adams returned to the United States in August 1817.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-Kaplan_2014_pages=307%E2%80%9311,_318%E2%80%9320-62)

## Secretary of State (1817–1825)

See also: [Presidency of James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_James_Monroe "Presidency of James Monroe")

Adams served as Secretary of State during Monroe's eight-year presidency, from 1817 to 1825. Many of his successes as secretary, such as the convention of 1818 with the United Kingdom, the Transcontinental Treaty with Spain, and the Monroe Doctrine, were not preplanned strategies but responses to unexpected events. Adams wanted to delay American recognition of the newly independent republics of Latin America to avoid the risk of war with Spain and its European allies. However, Andrew Jackson's military campaign in Florida and Henry Clay's threats in Congress forced Spain to cut a deal, which Adams negotiated successfully. Biographer James Lewis says, "He managed to play the cards that he had been dealt – cards that he very clearly had not wanted – in ways that forced the Spanish cabinet to recognize the weakness of its own hand".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-64) Apart from the Monroe doctrine, his last four years as Secretary of State were less successful because he was preoccupied with his presidential campaign and refused to make compromises with other countries that might have weakened his candidacy; the result was a small-scale trade war but a successful election to the White House.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/John_quincy_adams_-_thomas_sully.png/250px-John_quincy_adams_-_thomas_sully.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_quincy_adams_-_thomas_sully.png)

Painting of John Quincy Adams by [Thomas Sully](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sully "Thomas Sully"), 1824

Taking office in the aftermath of the War of 1812, Adams thought that the country had been fortunate in avoiding territorial losses, and he prioritized avoiding another war with a European power, particularly Britain.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-Kaplan_2014_pages=321%E2%80%9322-65) He also sought to avoid exacerbating sectional tensions, which had been a major issue for the country during the War of 1812.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-66)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-68) One of the major challenges confronting Adams was how to respond to the power vacuum in Latin America that arose from Spain's weakness following the [Peninsular War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_War "Peninsular War").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-69) In addition to his foreign policy role, Adams held several domestic duties, including overseeing the [1820 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1820_United_States_census "1820 United States census") and writing an extensive report on [weights and measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weights_and_measures "Weights and measures").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-70) The weights and measures report, a particular passion of Adams', provided an extensive historical perspective on the topic and advocated for adoption of the [metric system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_system "Metric system").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-71)

Monroe and Adams agreed on most major foreign policy issues: both favored neutrality in [Latin American independence wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_American_wars_of_independence "Spanish American wars of independence"), peace with the United Kingdom, rejection of a trade agreement with the French, and peaceful expansion into the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire")'s North American territories.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-72) The president and his secretary of state developed a strong working relationship, and while Adams often influenced Monroe's policies, he respected that Monroe made the final decisions on major issues.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-73) Monroe met regularly with his five-person [cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), which initially consisted of Adams, Secretary of the Treasury [William H. Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._Crawford "William H. Crawford"), Secretary of War [John C. Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Calhoun "John C. Calhoun"), Secretary of the Navy [Benjamin Crowninshield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Williams_Crowninshield "Benjamin Williams Crowninshield"), and Attorney General [William Wirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wirt_(Attorney_General) "William Wirt (Attorney General)").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-74) Adams developed a strong respect for Calhoun but believed that Crawford was unduly focused on succeeding Monroe in 1824.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-75)

During his time as minister to Britain, Adams had begun negotiations over several contentious issues that had not been solved by the War of 1812 or the Treaty of Ghent. In 1817, the two countries agreed to the [Rush–Bagot Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush%E2%80%93Bagot_Treaty "Rush–Bagot Treaty"), which limited naval armaments on the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes"). Negotiations between the two powers continued, resulting in the [Treaty of 1818](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_1818 "Treaty of 1818"), which defined the [Canada–United States border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93United_States_border "Canada–United States border") west of the Great Lakes. The boundary was set at the [49th parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_parallel_north "49th parallel north") to the [Rocky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains"), while the territory to the west of the mountains, known as [Oregon Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Country "Oregon Country"), would be jointly occupied. The agreement marked a watershed moment in [United Kingdom–United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom%E2%80%93United_States_relations "United Kingdom–United States relations") relations, as the United States focused on its southern and western borders and British concerns about American expansionism subsided.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-76)

### Adams–Onís Treaty

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Adams_onis_map.png/500px-Adams_onis_map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Adams_onis_map.png)

In the [Adams–Onís Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams%E2%80%93On%C3%ADs_Treaty "Adams–Onís Treaty"), the United States acquired Florida and set the western border of the 1803 [Louisiana Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase "Louisiana Purchase").

When Adams took office, Spanish possessions bordered the United States to the south and west. To the south, Spain retained control of [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Florida "Spanish Florida"), which the U.S. had long sought to purchase. Spain struggled to control the Indian tribes active in Florida, and some of those tribes raided United States territory. To the west, [New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain") bordered the territory acquired by the United States in the Louisiana Purchase, but no clear boundary had been established between United States and Spanish territory.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-Kaplan_2014_pages=321%E2%80%9322-65) After taking office, Adams began negotiations with [Luis de Onís](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_On%C3%ADs "Luis de Onís"), the Spanish minister to the United States, for the purchase of Florida and the settlement of a border between the United States and New Spain. The negotiations were interrupted by an escalation of the [Seminole War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminole_Wars "Seminole Wars"), and in December 1818, Monroe ordered General [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") to enter Florida and retaliate against [Seminoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminole "Seminole") that had raided Georgia. Exceeding his orders, Jackson captured the Spanish outposts of [St. Marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Marks,_Florida "St. Marks, Florida") and [Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensacola,_Florida "Pensacola, Florida") and [executed two British subjects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbuthnot_and_Ambrister_incident "Arbuthnot and Ambrister incident"). While Jackson's actions outraged the rest of the cabinet, Adams defended them as necessary to the country's self-defense, and he eventually convinced Monroe and most of the cabinet to support Jackson.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-Kaplan_2014_pages=333%E2%80%93337,_348-77) Adams informed Spain that its failure to police its own territory had compelled Jackson to act, and he advised Spain to either secure the region or sell it to the United States.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-78) The British, meanwhile, declined to risk their recent rapprochement with the United States, and did not make a major diplomatic issue out of Jackson's execution of the two men.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-79)

Negotiations between Spain and the United States continued, and Spain agreed to cede Florida. The determination of the western boundary of the United States proved more difficult. American expansionists favored setting the border at the [Rio Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Grande "Rio Grande"), but Spain, intent on protecting its colony of [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain") from American encroachment, insisted on setting the boundary at the [Sabine River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabine_River_(Texas%E2%80%93Louisiana) "Sabine River (Texas–Louisiana)"). At Monroe's direction, Adams agreed to the Sabine River boundary, but he insisted that Spain cede its claims on Oregon Country.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-80) Adams was deeply interested in establishing American control over the Oregon Country, partly because he believed that control of that region would spur trade with Asia. The acquisition of Spanish claims to the Pacific Northwest also allowed the Monroe administration to pair the acquisition of Florida, which was chiefly sought by Southerners, with territorial gains favored primarily by those in the North.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-81) After extended negotiations, Spain and the United States agreed to the [Adams–Onís Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams%E2%80%93On%C3%ADs_Treaty "Adams–Onís Treaty"), which was ratified in February 1821.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-Kaplan_2014_pages=333%E2%80%93337,_348-77) Adams was deeply proud of the treaty, though he privately was concerned by the potential expansion of slavery into the newly acquired territories.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-82) In 1824, the Monroe administration would strengthen US claims to Oregon by ratifying the [Russo-American Treaty of 1824](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-American_Treaty_of_1824 "Russo-American Treaty of 1824"), which established [Russian Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_America "Russian America")'s southern border at 54°40′ north.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-83)

### Monroe Doctrine

Main article: [Monroe Doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine "Monroe Doctrine")

As the Spanish Empire continued to fracture during Monroe's second term, Adams, Monroe and Clay became increasingly concerned that the "[Holy Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Alliance "Holy Alliance")" of [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia "Prussia"), Austria, and Russia would seek to bring Spain's erstwhile colonies under their control, to the point of even contemplating a Holy Alliance of their own to defend democracy. In his 1821 Fourth of July address, Adams addressed this issue, noting a shared "chain of sympathy" between the U.S. and Latin America, but arguing for neutrality rather than a Holy Alliance.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-84) In 1822, following the conclusion of the Adams–Onís Treaty, the Monroe administration recognized the independence of several Latin American countries, including [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") and Mexico. In 1823, British Foreign Secretary [George Canning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Canning "George Canning") suggested that the United States and Britain should work together to preserve the independence of these fledgling republics. The cabinet debated whether to accept the offer, but Adams opposed it. Instead, Adams urged Monroe to publicly declare the United States' opposition to any European attempt to colonize or re-take control of territory in the Americas, while also committing the United States to neutrality in European affairs. In his December 1823 [annual message to Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Union "State of the Union"), Monroe laid out the Monroe Doctrine, which was largely built upon Adams's ideas.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kaplan380385-85) In issuing the Monroe Doctrine, the United States displayed a new level of assertiveness in international relations, as the doctrine represented the country's first claim to a [sphere of influence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_of_influence "Sphere of influence"). It also marked the country's shift in psychological orientation away from Europe and towards the Americas. Debates over foreign policy would no longer center on relations with Britain and France, but instead focus on western expansion and relations with Native Americans.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-86) The doctrine became one of the foundational principles of [U.S. foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_U.S._foreign_policy "History of U.S. foreign policy").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kaplan380385-85)

## 1824 presidential election

Main article: [1824 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1824_United_States_presidential_election "1824 United States presidential election")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/ElectoralCollege1824.svg/250px-ElectoralCollege1824.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1824.svg)

1824 presidential election results

Immediately upon becoming Secretary of State, Adams emerged as one of Monroe's most likely successors, as the last three presidents had all served in the role before taking office. As the [1824 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1824_United_States_presidential_election "1824 United States presidential election") approached, Henry Clay, John C. Calhoun (who later dropped out of the race), and William H. Crawford appeared to be Adams's primary competition to succeed Monroe.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-87) Crawford favored state sovereignty and a [strict constructionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strict_constructionist "Strict constructionist") view of the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution"), while Clay, Calhoun, and Adams embraced federally funded [internal improvements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_improvements "Internal improvements"), high [tariffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariffs_in_United_States_history "Tariffs in United States history"), and the [Second Bank of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bank_of_the_United_States "Second Bank of the United States"), which was also known as the national bank.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-Howe_2007_203%E2%80%93204-88) Because the Federalist Party had all but collapsed after the War of 1812, all the major presidential candidates were members of the Democratic-Republican Party.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-parsons7072-89) Adams felt that his own election as president would vindicate his father, while also allowing him to pursue an ambitious domestic policy. Though he lacked the charisma of his competitors, Adams was widely respected and benefited from the lack of other prominent Northern political leaders.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-90)

Adams's top choice for the role of vice president was General Andrew Jackson; Adams noted that "the Vice-Presidency was a station in which [Jackson] could hang no one, and in which he would need to quarrel with no one".[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-91) However, as the 1824 election approached, Jackson jumped into the race for president, and Calhoun ended up receiving the Vice-presidential support of Adams supporters.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-parsons7072-89) While the other candidates based their candidacies on their long tenure as congressmen, diplomats, or members of the cabinet, Jackson's appeal rested on his military service, especially in the [Battle of New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_New_Orleans "Battle of New Orleans").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-92) The [congressional nominating caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_nominating_caucus "Congressional nominating caucus") had decided upon previous Democratic-Republican presidential nominees, but it had become largely discredited by 1824. Candidates were instead nominated by state legislatures or nominating conventions, and Adams received the endorsement of the New England legislatures.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-93) The regional strength of each candidate played an important role in the election; Adams was popular in [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England"), Clay and Jackson were strong in the West, and Jackson and Crawford competed for the South.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kaplan386389-94)

| States for Adams | States for Jackson | States for Crawford |
| * Connecticut * Illinois * Kentucky * Louisiana * Maine * Maryland * Massachusetts * Missouri * New Hampshire * New York * Ohio * Rhode Island * Vermont | * Alabama * Indiana * Mississippi * New Jersey * Pennsylvania * South Carolina * Tennessee | * Delaware * Georgia * North Carolina * Virginia |

In the 1824 presidential election, Jackson won a plurality in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States) "Electoral College (United States)"), taking 99 of the 261 electoral votes, while Adams won 84, Crawford won 41, and Clay took 37. Calhoun, meanwhile, won a majority of the electoral votes for vice president.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kaplan386389-94) Adams nearly swept the electoral votes of New England and won a majority of the electoral votes in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), but he won just six electoral votes from the slave states. Most of Jackson's support came from slave-holding states, but he also won [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), and some electoral votes from the Northwest.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-95) As no candidate won a majority of the electoral votes, the House was required to hold a contingent election under the terms of the [Twelfth Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelfth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twelfth Amendment to the United States Constitution"). The House would decide among the top three electoral vote winners, with each state's delegation having one vote; thus, unlike his three rivals, Clay was not eligible to be elected by the House.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kaplan386389-94)

Adams knew that his own victory in the contingent election would require the support of Clay, who wielded immense influence in the House of Representatives.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-96) Though they were quite different in temperament and had clashed in the past, Adams and Clay shared similar views on national issues. By contrast, Clay viewed Jackson as a dangerous [demagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demagogue "Demagogue"), and he was unwilling to support Crawford due to the latter's health issues.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-97) Adams and Clay met before the contingent election, and Clay agreed to support Adams in the election.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kap391393-98) Adams also met with Federalists such as [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster"), promising that he would not deny governmental positions to members of their party.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-99) On February 9, 1825, Adams won the contingent election on the first ballot, taking 13 of the 24 state delegations. Adams won the House delegations of all the states in which he or Clay had won a majority of the electoral votes, as well as the delegations of [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), and [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kap391393-98) Adams's victory made him the first child of a president to serve as president himself.[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-100) After the election, many of Jackson's supporters claimed that Adams and Clay had reached a "[Corrupt bargain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrupt_bargain "Corrupt bargain")" whereby Adams promised Clay the position of Secretary of State in return for Clay's support.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-kap391393-98)

## Presidency (1825–1829)

Main article: [Presidency of John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_John_Quincy_Adams "Presidency of John Quincy Adams")

### Inauguration

Adams was [inaugurated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_John_Quincy_Adams "Inauguration of John Quincy Adams") on March 4, 1825, becoming the first son of a former United States president to himself become president, a feat only repeated 176 years later by [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), son of George H. W. Bush. As Adams took the [oath of office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oath_of_office_of_the_president_of_the_United_States#Use_of_Bibles "Oath of office of the president of the United States"), he departed from tradition by placing his hand on a book of [constitutional law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_law "Constitutional law") instead of on a [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible "Bible").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-101) In his inaugural address, he adopted a post-partisan tone, promising to avoid party-building and politically motivated appointments. He also proposed an elaborate program of "internal improvements": roads, ports, and canals. Though some were worried about the constitutionality of such federal projects, Adams argued that the [General Welfare Clause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxing_and_Spending_Clause "Taxing and Spending Clause") provided for broad constitutional authority. He promised that he would ask Congress to authorize many such projects.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams#cite_note-102)

Thomas Jefferson (April 13 [O.S. April 2], 1743 – July 4, 1826) was a Founding Father and the third president of the United States, serving from 1801 to 1809. From 1797 to 1801, he served as the second vice president under John Adams. A prolific writer and philosopher, Jefferson was the primary author of the Declaration of Independence. His political philosophy, defined by republicanism, individual liberty, agrarianism, and limited government, formed the basis for Jeffersonian democracy. While he remains celebrated as an icon of American political values, Jefferson is also controversial for having enslaved more than 600 people.

Jefferson was born in Shadwell, Virginia. During the American Revolution, Jefferson represented Virginia in the Second Continental Congress. His advocacy for individual rights, including the freedoms of thought, speech, and religion, helped shape the ideological foundations of the revolution.[3][4] Jefferson served as the second governor of Virginia from 1779 to 1781. In 1785, Congress appointed him as U.S. Minister to France, where he served from 1785 to 1789. President George Washington then appointed Jefferson the nation's first secretary of state, where he served from 1790 to 1793. In 1792, Jefferson and political ally James Madison organized the Democratic-Republican Party to oppose the Federalist Party during the formation of the nation's First Party System. Jefferson and Federalist John Adams became both personal friends and political rivals. In the 1796 U.S. presidential election between the two, Jefferson came in second, which made him Adams' vice president under the electoral laws of the time. Four years later, in the 1800 presidential election, he again challenged Adams and won the presidency. When running for reelection in 1804, Jefferson overwhelmingly defeated the Federalists' Charles Cotesworth Pinckney of South Carolina.

Jefferson's presidency assertively defended the nation's shipping and trade interests against Barbary pirates and aggressive British trade policies, promoted a western expansionist policy with the Louisiana Purchase, which doubled the nation's geographic size, and reduced military forces and expenditures following successful negotiations with France. In his second presidential term, he was beset by difficulties at home, including the trial of his former vice president Aaron Burr. In 1807, Jefferson implemented the Embargo Act to defend the nation's industries from British threats to U.S. shipping, limit foreign trade, and stimulate the birth of American manufacturing.

Jefferson is ranked among the upper tier of U.S. presidents both by scholars and in public opinion. Presidential scholars and historians have praised Jefferson's advocacy of religious freedom and tolerance, his peaceful acquisition of the Louisiana Territory from France, and his leadership in supporting the Lewis and Clark Expedition. They acknowledge his lifelong ownership of large numbers of slaves, but offer varying interpretations of his views on and relationship with slavery.[5]

Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743 (April 2, 1743, Old Style, Julian calendar), at the family's Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia. He was the third of ten children.[6] His father, Peter Jefferson, was a planter and surveyor; his mother was Jane Randolph.[b] Peter Jefferson moved his family to Tuckahoe Plantation in 1745 following the death of William Randolph III, the plantation's owner and Jefferson's friend, who in his will had named Peter guardian of Randolph's children. The Jeffersons returned to Shadwell before October 1753.[9]

Jefferson began his education together with the Randolph children at Tuckahoe under tutors.[10] Thomas' father Peter, who was self-taught and regretted not having a formal education, entered Thomas into an English school at age five. In 1752, at age nine, he attended a local school run by a Presbyterian minister and also began studying the natural world, which he grew to love. He studied Latin, Greek, and French, and began learning to ride horses. Thomas read books from his father's modest library.[11] He was taught from 1758 to 1760 by the Reverend James Maury near Gordonsville, Virginia, where he studied history, science, and the classics while boarding with Maury's family.[11][12] Jefferson came to know various Native Americans including Cherokee chief Ostenaco, who often stopped at Shadwell to visit on their way to Williamsburg to trade.[13][14] In Williamsburg, the young Jefferson met and came to admire Patrick Henry.[15]

Thomas's father died in 1757, and his estate was divided between his sons, Thomas and Randolph.[16] John Harvie Sr. became 14-year-old Thomas' guardian.[17] Thomas inherited approximately 5,000 acres (7.8 sq mi; 20.2 km2), which included the land on which he later built Monticello in 1772.[18]

In 1761, at the age of seventeen, Jefferson entered the College of William & Mary in Williamsburg, where he studied mathematics and philosophy with William Small. Under Small's tutelage, Jefferson encountered the ideas of British empiricists, including John Locke, Francis Bacon, and Isaac Newton. Small also introduced Jefferson to George Wythe and Francis Fauquier. Small, Wythe, and Fauquier recognized Jefferson as a man of exceptional ability and included him in their inner circle, where he became a regular member of their Friday dinner parties. Jefferson later wrote that, while there, he "heard more common good sense, more rational & philosophical conversations than in all the rest of my life".[19]

During his first year in college, Jefferson spent considerable time attending parties and dancing and was not very frugal with his expenditures; in his second year, regretting that he had squandered away time and money in his first year, he committed to studying fifteen hours a day.[20] While at William & Mary, Jefferson became a member of the Flat Hat Club, the nation's oldest secret society, a small group whose members included St. George Tucker, Edmund Randolph, and James Innes.[21][22]

Jefferson concluded his formal studies in April 1762.[23] He read the law under Wythe's tutelage while working as a law clerk in his office.[24] Jefferson was well-read in a broad variety of subjects, including law, philosophy, history, natural law, natural religion, ethics,[citation needed] and several areas of science, including astronomy[25] and agriculture.

Jefferson kept two commonplace books: from about age 15 to 30, he compiled a book of sayings and quotations, published in the 20th century as Jefferson's Literary Commonplace Book.[26] During his years of legal study under Wythe, Jefferson began recording his notes on law, history, and philosophy, and continued to do so until the end of his life; his Legal Commonplace Book was also published in the 20th century.[27]

On July 20, 1765, Jefferson's sister Martha married his close friend and college companion Dabney Carr, which greatly pleased Jefferson. In October of that year, however, Jefferson's sister Jane unexpectedly died at age 25. Her death plunged Jefferson into a months-long period of mourning that was spoken of amongst the family.[28]

Jefferson treasured his books and amassed three sizable libraries in his lifetime. He began assembling his first library, which grew to 200 volumes, in his youth.[29] Wythe was so impressed with Jefferson that he later bequeathed his entire library to him.[30] In 1770, however, Jefferson's first library was destroyed in a fire at his Shadwell home. His second library, which replenished the first, grew to nearly 6,500 volumes by 1814.[31] After British forces set the Library of Congress on fire in the Burning of Washington in 1814, Jefferson sold his second library to the U.S. government for $23,950, hoping to help jumpstart the Library of Congress's rebuilding. Jefferson used a portion of the proceeds to pay off some of his large debt. Jefferson soon resumed collecting his third personal library. In a letter to John Adams, Jefferson wrote, "I cannot live without books."[32][33] By the time of Jefferson's death a decade later, his third and final library had grown to nearly 2,000 volumes.[34]
